newsitem.title: USA: One-third of Georgia schools plan tax vote.
newsitem.headline: One-third of Georgia schools plan tax vote.

text.p: Sixty-seven of Georgia's 180 school districts have scheduled March 18 referendums on proposals to raise sales taxes to build new schools or retire outstanding debt, state school officials said Tuesday.
The March election date was the earliest the local elections could be held under a constitutional amendment approved by voters statewide in November.
The new law allows districts to levy a one-cent local option sales tax for five years to fund capital projects or retire construction debt.
Pat Sandor, a spokesman for the state school superintendent's office, said the flurry of referendums was unsurprising.
"I think a number of them saw this as an option to retire existing bonds and to execute projects that were already in the works or in the planning stages," said Sandor.
The home mortgage market has seen a similar trend, he said.

"Everybody today, coast to coast across the nation, has been refinancng their 30-year mortgages into 15-year plans because they're saving a lot of money by cutting the time cost of borrowing," Sandor said. "I suspect a lot of local school boards looked at this in the exact same way. It appears that for most, this is a model of fiscal responsibility."
Georgia school districts have traditionally financed construction with long-term bonds backed mainly by property taxes.

Fulton County school officials calculated they could cut total costs nearly in half by using pay-as-you-go sales tax revenues instead of 30-year bond financing to add 17 schools and renovate dozens. With bonds, the cost over 30 years would total $790 million.
By shifting some of the school building debt to sales taxes, the cost could also be spread among visitors rather than borne solely by local property owners, Sandor said.
For that reason, "every municipality that has a major thoroughfare through it," has scheduled a March 18 referendum, Sandor said.
State officials said they could not predict how many of the referendums would pass, since all are local and building needs varied.
Some have lobbied heavily, including DeKalb, where even elementary school children have helped make yard signs urging voters to approve the plan.
Sandor said some districts could comeout even farther ahead by investing the sales tax revenues short-term until the money is needed to pay construction bills.
The ballots must spell out specific projects, so districts could not collect the tax and decide later how to spend the revenue.

In districts where the referendums are countywide, city school systems within the county would share the revenues. In elections called by city school districts, the surrounding county would not share funds, Sandor said.
Cities scheduling March 18 referendums are Atlanta, Bremen, Buford, Cartersville, Chickamauga, Commerce, Dalton, Decatur, Jefferson, Pelhame, Trion and Vidalia.

Counties holding referendums are Atkinson, Baldwin, Barrow, Bartow, bleckley, Brantley, Butts, Catoosa, Chattoga, Clarke, Clay, Clayton, Coffee, Columbia, Cook, Coweta, Crisp, Dade, Dawson, Dekalb, Douglas, Elbert, Emanuel, Forsyth, Fulton, Glascock and Gwinnett.

Other counties are Haralson, Hart, Houston, Irwin, Jackson, Jasper, Jefferson, Liberty, Macon, McDuffie, Meriwether, Mitchell, Murray, Paulding, Pickens, Pierce, Pike, Richmond, Screven, Spalding, Taylor, Tift, Toombs, Troup, Twiggs, Walker and Whitfield.
--Jane Sutton, 305-374-5013
